# Hydrostatic Equilibrium and the Virial Theorem {#sec-hydro}

## The virial theorem

We consider a self-gravitating cloud of gas in equilibrium, described by the momentum equation in conservation form (@eq-conserv-ch6-eq-momentum)
$$
\frac{\partial (\rho \vb{v})}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot [\rho
\vb{v} \otimes \vb{v}+ p\vb{I}] = - \rho \nabla \Psi,
$$ {#eq-hydro-1}
where $\Psi$ is the gravitational potential. We consider the scalar moment of inertia
$$
I = \frac{1}{2} \int_V \rho (\vb{r}) r^2 \dd V,
$$ {#eq-hydro-2}
where $V$ is a volume that encloses the whole gas cloud. The time derivative of $I$ is (using the continuity equation)
$$
\begin{alignedat}{2}
\frac{\dd I}{\dd t} &{}={} && \frac{1}{2}  \int_V \frac{\partial
\rho}{\partial t} r^2 \dd V \\
&{}={} && - \frac{1}{2} \int_V \nabla \cdot (\rho
\vb{v}) r^2 \dd V \\
&{}={} && - \frac{1}{2} \int_V \nabla \cdot (\rho \vb{v}r^2) \dd V \\
&&& + \frac{1}{2}  \int_V \rho \vb{v} \cdot \nabla r^2 \dd V.
\end{alignedat}
$$ {#eq-hydro-3}
The total divergence term is equal to a boundary integral
$$
\int_V \nabla \cdot (\rho \vb{v}r^2) \dd V = \int_{\partial V} \rho
\vb{v}r^2 \cdot \vb{n} \dd A,
$$ {#eq-hydro-4}
but the latter vanishes since, by assumption, $\rho \rightarrow 0$ at the boundary of $V$. So we find
$$
\frac{\dd I}{\dd t} = \frac{1}{2}  \int_V \rho \vb{v} \cdot \nabla
r^2 \dd V = \int_V \rho \vb{v} \cdot \vb{r} \dd V.
$$ {#eq-hydro-5}
Here, we have used the fact that $\nabla r =\vb{r}/ r$.

The second time derivative of $I$ is
$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\dd^2 I}{\dd t^2} &= \int_V \frac{\partial (\rho \vb{v})}{\partial t} \cdot \vb{r} \dd V \\
&= - \int_V \rho \nabla \Psi \cdot \vb{r} \dd V \\
&\qquad - \int_V \nabla \cdot [\rho \vb{v} \otimes \vb{v}+ p\vb{I}] \cdot \vb{r} \dd V \\
&= - \int_V \rho \nabla \Psi \cdot \vb{r} \dd V \\
&\qquad - \int_V \nabla \cdot [\rho (\vb{v} \cdot \vb{r}) \vb{v}+ p\vb{r}] \dd V \\
&\qquad + \int_V [\rho \vb{v} \otimes \vb{v}+ p\vb{I}] : \nabla \vb{r} \dd V,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-hydro-6}
where the notation $\vb{A}: \vb{B}$ denotes the inner product between two tensors:
$$
\vb{A}: \vb{B}= \sum_{i = 1}^3 \sum_{k = 1}^3 A_{i k} B_{k i} =
\mathrm{Trace} \left[ \left(\begin{array}{ccc}
A_{x x} & A_{x y} & A_{x z}\\
A_{y x} & A_{y y} & A_{y z}\\
A_{z x} & A_{z y} & A_{z z}
\end{array}\right)  \left(\begin{array}{ccc}
B_{x x} & B_{x y} & B_{x z}\\
B_{y x} & B_{y y} & B_{y z}\\
B_{z x} & B_{z y} & B_{z z}
\end{array}\right) \right] .
$$ {#eq-hydro-7}
Once again, we can drop the total divergence terms, since, by the divergence theorem, they are equal to boundary integrals that vanish because $\rho$ and $p$ vanish at the boundary of $V$. We find
$$
\frac{\dd^2 I}{\dd t^2} = - \int_V \rho \nabla \Psi \cdot
\vb{r} \dd V + \int_V [\rho \vb{v} \otimes \vb{v}+
p\vb{I}] : \nabla \vb{r} \dd V.
$$ {#eq-hydro-virial-base}
The second term in the RHS is simpler than it looks, because
$$
\nabla \vb{r}= \left(\begin{array}{ccc}
\partial_x x & \partial_x y & \partial_x z\\
\partial_y x & \partial_y y & \partial_y z\\
\partial_z x & \partial_z y & \partial_z z
\end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{ccc}
1 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 1 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{array}\right) =\vb{I}.
$$ {#eq-hydro-9}
So everything simplifies to
$$
\int_V [\rho \vb{v} \otimes \vb{v}+ p\vb{I}] : \nabla \vb{r}
\dd V = \int_V \rho v^2 \dd V + 3 \int_V p \dd V =: 2 K +
3 \Pi,
$$ {#eq-hydro-10}
where $K$ is the kinetic energy of the gas and $\Pi$ is the integrated pressure.

The first term in the RHS of @eq-hydro-virial-base requires a little more work. First, we need to compute an expression for the gravitational potential in terms of the mass density $\rho$. To do this, we remember that the gravitational potential generated by a distribution of point masses with mass $m_i$ at locations $\vb{r}_i$ is given by
$$
\Psi (\vb{r}) = - \sum_{i = 1}^N \frac{Gm_i}{ | \vb{r}-\vb{r}_i
|} .
$$ {#eq-hydro-11}
This can be generalized to the case of a mass density distribution by converting the sum into an integral
$$
\Psi (\vb{r}) = - \int_V \frac{G \rho (\vb{r}')}{ |
\vb{r}-\vb{r}' |} \dd^3 r' .
$$ {#eq-hydro-12}
Inserting this into the first term in the RHS of @eq-hydro-virial-base yields
$$
\int_V \rho \nabla \Psi \cdot \vb{r} \dd^3 r = - \int_V
\dd^3 r \rho (\vb{r}) \nabla_{\vb{r}} \int_V \dd^3
r'  \frac{G \rho (\vb{r}')}{ | \vb{r}-\vb{r}' |} \cdot
\vb{r},
$$ {#eq-hydro-derivative-of-potential}
where we have used the notation $\nabla_{\vb{r}}$ to remind ourselves that the derivatives are computed with respect to the unprimed position $\vb{r}$. In particular, note that $\rho (\vb{r}')$ in the integral is not affected by the derivative, since it is a function of $\vb{r}'$ and not of $\vb{r}$. The only term that we need to differentiate is the denominator:
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \nabla_{\vb{r}} \frac{1}{| \vb{r}-\vb{r}' |} \\
& \quad = \nabla_{\vb{r}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{(x - x')^2 + (y - y')^2 + (z - z')^2}} \\
& \quad = \frac{- 1}{[(x - x')^2 + (y - y')^2 + (z - z')^2]^{3 / 2}} \\
& \qquad\quad \times \left(\begin{array}{c}
x - x' \\
y - y' \\
z - z'
\end{array}\right) \\
& \quad = - \frac{\vb{r}-\vb{r}'}{| \vb{r}-\vb{r}' |^3} .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-hydro-diff-one-over-r}
Inserting the last expression into @eq-hydro-derivative-of-potential, we obtain
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \int_V \rho \nabla \Psi \cdot \vb{r} \dd^3 r \\
& \quad = \int_V \dd^3 r \int_V \dd^3 r' \frac{G \rho (\vb{r}') \rho (\vb{r}) }{ | \vb{r}-\vb{r}' |^3} (\vb{r}-\vb{r}') \cdot \vb{r} \\
& \quad = \int_V \dd^3 r \int_V \dd^3 r' \frac{G \rho (\vb{r}') \rho (\vb{r}) }{ | \vb{r}-\vb{r}' |^3} | \vb{r}-\vb{r}' |^2 \\
& \qquad + \int_V \dd^3 r \int_V \dd^3 r' \frac{G \rho (\vb{r}') \rho (\vb{r}) }{ | \vb{r}-\vb{r}' |^3} (\vb{r}-\vb{r}') \cdot \vb{r}' \\
& \quad = \int_V \dd^3 r \int_V \dd^3 r' \frac{G \rho (\vb{r}') \rho (\vb{r}) }{| \vb{r}-\vb{r}' |} \\
& \qquad + \int_V \dd^3 r' \rho (\vb{r}') \vb{r}' \cdot \int_V \dd^3 r \frac{G \rho (\vb{r}) (\vb{r}-\vb{r}') }{ | \vb{r}-\vb{r}' |^3} \\
& \quad = - \int_V \dd^3 r \Psi (\vb{r}) \rho (\vb{r}) \\
& \qquad - \int_V \rho (\vb{r}') \nabla_{\vb{r}'} \Psi (\vb{r}') \cdot \vb{r}' \dd^3 r' .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-hydro-expansion-of-grad-potential}
We have used the fact that (note the difference in sign compared to @eq-hydro-diff-one-over-r)
$$
\nabla_{\vb{r}'}  \frac{1}{| \vb{r}-\vb{r}' |} =
\frac{\vb{r}-\vb{r}'}{| \vb{r}-\vb{r}' |^3} .
$$ {#eq-hydro-16}
The last term on the RHS of @eq-hydro-expansion-of-grad-potential is identical to the LHS, so we find
$$
- \int_V \rho \nabla \Psi \cdot \vb{r} \dd^3 r= \frac{1}{2}
\int_V \dd^3 r \Psi (\vb{r}) \rho (\vb{r}) = W,
$$ {#eq-hydro-17}
$W$ being the gravitational potential energy.

For a **stationary configuration** $\dd^2 I / \dd t^2 = 0$, so @eq-hydro-virial-base yields the *virial theorem*:
$$
\boxed{W + 2 K + 3 \Pi = 0.}
$$ {#eq-hydro-virial-theorem}
For an ideal gas $p = (\Gamma - 1) \rho \varepsilon$ (@eq-thermo-gamma-law), so
$$
\Pi = \int_V p \dd V = (\Gamma - 1) \int_V \rho \varepsilon \dd V =
(\Gamma - 1) U,
$$ {#eq-hydro-19}
where $U$ is the total internal energy. In this case, the virial theorem reads
$$
\boxed{W + 2 K + 3 (\Gamma - 1) U = 0.}
$$ {#eq-hydro-virial-ideal-gas}

## Hydrostatic equilibria

A fluid is in hydrostatic equilibrium when $\vb{v} = 0$, so that Euler's equation reduces to $\nabla p = - \rho \nabla \Psi$. For a spherical star, this reads $\dd p / \dd r = - G M (r) \rho / r^2$, where $M (r)$ is the mass enclosed within the radius $r$ (see also @eq-euler-hydrostatic-equilibrium).

The virial theorem has an important consequence for the stability of hydrostatic equilibria. Consider a cloud of gas or star in hydrostatic equilibrium, that is with no large scale motion (no rotation). Then the virial theorem states that
$$
W + 3 (\Gamma - 1) U = 0.
$$ {#eq-hydro-virial-simple}
On the other hand, the energy of the cloud is
$$
E = W + U.
$$ {#eq-hydro-energy}
The energy must be negative for the system to be bound, $E \leq 0$. This implies
$$
U \leq - W = 3 (\Gamma - 1) U \Longrightarrow [- 1 + 3 (\Gamma -
1)] U \geq 0,
$$ {#eq-hydro-23}
since $U \geq 0$, this requires
$$
\Gamma \geq 4 / 3.
$$ {#eq-hydro-24}
Monoatomic gas has $\Gamma = 5 / 3$, so regular stars are stable. Matter dominated by relativistic particles, such as radiation or the relativistic degenerate electrons in white dwarfs and in the iron cores of massive stars, has $\Gamma \approx 4 / 3$. Stars made of such matter are only marginally stable, and small effects that reduce $\Gamma$ below $4/3$ can make them collapse. This happens in the iron cores of massive stars, where electron captures reduce the pressure, triggering core-collapse supernovae (@sec-sn and @sec-euler-worksheet), and in very massive stars, where the production of electron–positron pairs triggers so-called pair-instability supernovae.

A surprising consequence of the virial theorem is that self-gravitating systems have *negative specific heat*. Consider a self-gravitating cloud (a protostar) emitting infrared radiation. As its energy $E$ becomes more negative its gravitational binding energy $- W$ must increase, because $U \geq 0$. We can use @eq-hydro-virial-simple and @eq-hydro-energy to solve for $U$ in terms of $E$:
$$
U = - \frac{E}{3 \Gamma - 4} .
$$ {#eq-hydro-internal-energy-from-virial}
If $\Gamma > 4 / 3$, @eq-hydro-internal-energy-from-virial predicts that $U$ will increase as $E$ becomes more negative. Meaning that the system heats up as it loses energy! Eventually the cloud contracts to the point that nuclear fusion starts occurring and a star is born. Nuclear burning *prevents* the star from heating up further.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Example

Could the Sun be powered by gravitational contraction alone? In this case, the Sun would radiate its gravitational binding energy, $| W | \sim G M_{\odot}^2 / R_{\odot}$, over a time
$$
t_{\mathrm{KH}} \sim \frac{G M_{\odot}^2}{R_{\odot} L_{\odot}} \approx 3 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{yr},
$$ {#eq-hydro-kelvin-helmholtz}
where $L_{\odot} \approx 3.8 \times 10^{26}\,\mathrm{W}$ ($3.8 \times 10^{33}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$) is the luminosity of the Sun. This is the so-called *Kelvin–Helmholtz time*. It is much shorter than the age of the Earth, about $4.5 \times 10^9$ years, so the Sun must have another source of energy: nuclear fusion.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Example

The hot gas in a galaxy cluster is in approximate virial equilibrium in the gravitational potential of the cluster. Consider a cluster with mass $M \sim 10^{15}\,M_{\odot}$ and radius $R \sim 1\,\mathrm{Mpc}$, and assume, for simplicity, that the gas has the same distribution as the total mass. For a uniform sphere $W = - \frac{3}{5} G M^2 / R$, while $3 \Pi = 3 M k_B T / (\mu m_u)$, so the virial theorem gives
$$
k_B T \sim \frac{G M \mu m_u}{5 R} \approx 5\,\mathrm{keV},
$$ {#eq-hydro-cluster-temperature}
or $T \sim 6 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{K}$, where we have taken $\mu \approx 0.6$ for fully ionized gas. This is why galaxy clusters are bright X-ray sources, as in the case of the Bullet cluster (@fig-continua-bullet-cluster).
:::

## Application to star formation

Consider a spherical cloud of radius $R$. For simplicity, we take its density $\bar{\rho}$ to be uniform. Then the gravitational potential energy is
$$
- W = G \int_0^R 4 \pi r \rho (r) M (r) \dd r = \frac{16 \pi^2}{15} G \bar{\rho}^2 R^5 = \frac{3}{5} \frac{G M^2}{R},
$$ {#eq-hydro-28}
where $M = \frac{4 \pi}{3} \bar{\rho} R^3$ is the mass of the cloud and
$$
M (r) = \int_0^r 4 \pi r'^2 \rho (r') \dd r'
$$ {#eq-hydro-29}
is the mass enclosed within the radius $r$. For an ideal gas, the pressure is given by
$$
p = \frac{k_B T}{\mu m_u} \rho,
$$ {#eq-hydro-30}
where $\mu$ is the mean molecular weight (@eq-continua-mu), $m_u$ is the atomic mass unit, $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant and $T$ is the temperature. We can assume $T$ to be constant. This is a good approximation for optically thin clouds which can efficiently cool by emitting radiation. With this approximation
$$
\Pi = \int_0^R 4 \pi r^2 p (r) \dd r = \frac{4}{3} \pi c_s^2
\bar{\rho} R^3,
$$ {#eq-hydro-31}
where
$$
c_s^2 = \frac{k_B T}{\mu m_u}
$$ {#eq-hydro-32}
is a constant. As we will see later, $c_s$ turns out to be the sound speed of the gas (@sec-sound). The condition for collapse of the cloud is that $3 \Pi < | W |$, which implies that collapse will occur for a cloud with
$$
R > R_J, \qquad R_J^2 = \frac{15 c_s^2}{4 \pi G \bar{\rho}} .
$$ {#eq-hydro-33}
$R_J$ is called the *Jeans length*. Typical molecular clouds have $R \gg R_J$, so instead of collapsing to an object with mass equal to the mass of the cloud, they fragment into smaller pieces. The mass of these fragments can be estimated as the mass contained within one Jeans length, the so-called *Jeans mass*[^hydro-2]:
$$
\begin{aligned}
M_J &= \frac{4 \pi}{3}  \bar{\rho} R_J^3 = \frac{15^{3 / 2} c_s^3}{3 (4 \pi
\bar{\rho})^{1 / 2} G^{3 / 2}} \\
&= \frac{15^{3 / 2} k_B^{3 / 2}}{3 (4 \pi)^{1 / 2} m_u^2
G^{3 / 2}}  \frac{T^{3 / 2}}{\mu^2 n^{1 / 2}} .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-hydro-34}
Inserting the values of the constants, we find
$$
M_J \approx 94\,M_{\odot}  \left( \frac{T}{\mathrm{K}} \right)^{3 / 2}
\left( \frac{\mathrm{cm}^{- 3}}{n} \right)^{1 / 2}  \frac{1}{\mu^2} .
$$ {#eq-hydro-jeans-mass}
For a typical molecular cloud with $T = 10\,\mathrm{K}$, $n = 100\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}$, and $\mu = 2$ (for molecular hydrogen) the Jeans length is $R_J \approx 1.5\,\mathrm{pc}$ and the Jeans mass is $M_J \approx 70\,M_{\odot}$. This is much larger than the mass of a typical star. Note however that the Jeans mass decreases with increasing $n$. So, as long as the gas can efficiently cool and remain at low temperature, the fragments collapse and undergo further fragmentation. In the dense cores of molecular clouds, with $n \sim 10^4\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}$, the Jeans mass is $M_J \approx 7\,M_{\odot}$, and at even higher densities it approaches the mass of typical stars.

While the arguments we have given here give an order of magnitude estimate for the mass of protostars, star formation is strongly influenced by a number of factors that we have neglected. These include turbulence and magnetic fields. Moreover, star formation strongly depends on the ability of the gas to cool to low temperature, as shown by @eq-hydro-jeans-mass.

## In-class worksheet {#sec-hydro-worksheet}

For a magnetic star the virial theorem becomes:
$$
W + 2 K + 3 \Pi +\mathfrak{M}= 0,
$$ {#eq-hydro-ws1}
where the new term is the magnetic energy of the star, which is
$$
\mathfrak{M}= \frac{1}{2 \mu_0} \int B^2 \dd V .
$$ {#eq-hydro-ws2}

1.  Find the condition for stability of a nonrotating star in terms of $\Gamma$ and $\mathfrak{M}$.

2.  What is the maximum magnetic field strength for a Sun-like star ($R = 7 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{km}$, $M = 2 \times 10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}$)? Neglect factors of order unity, and give the answer in tesla and in gauss ($1\,\mathrm{T} = 10^4\,\mathrm{G}$).

3.  What is the maximum magnetic field strength for a neutron star ($R = 12\,\mathrm{km}$, $M = 3 \times 10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}$)?

## Exercises {#sec-hydro-exercises}

::: {#exr-hydro-slab}
## Self-gravitating slab

An infinite, static slab of incompressible fluid with uniform density $\rho_0$ fills the region $| z | < a$ and is held together by its own gravity.

1.  Compute the gravitational acceleration inside and outside the slab, and the pressure profile inside it. Use Poisson's equation, $\nabla^2 \Psi = 4 \pi G \rho$.

2.  Model the disk of a galaxy as such a slab, with $\rho_0 = 10^{-23}\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}} = 10^{-20}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ and $a = 10^{19}\,\mathrm{m}$. A star starts at rest at $z = a$. How fast does it cross the mid-plane, and what is the period of its vertical oscillation?

Adapted from @clarke2007, Problem 8.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
::: {.solution}
1.  The Poisson equation reads
    $$
    \partial_z^2 \Psi (z) = 4 \pi G \rho (z) .
    $$
    By symmetry, we can assume $\partial_z \Psi (0) = 0$. We can then integrate the Poisson equation to find
    $$
    \partial_z \Psi (z) = 4 \pi G \int_0^z \rho (z') \dd z' = 4 \pi G \rho_0
    \left\{\begin{array}{ll}
    z, & z < a,\\
    a, & z \geq a.
    \end{array}\right.
    $$
    Since the potential is unique up to a constant, we can also set $\Psi (0) = 0$. A second integration of Poisson equation then yields
    $$
    \Psi (z) = 2 \pi G \rho_0  \left\{\begin{array}{ll}
    z^2, & z < a,\\
    a (2 z - a), & z \geq a.
    \end{array}\right.
    $$
    The gravitational acceleration is $g_z = - \partial_z \Psi$, that is, $g_z = - 4 \pi G \rho_0 z$ inside the slab and $g_z = - 4 \pi G \rho_0 a$ for $z \geq a$ (and $+ 4 \pi G \rho_0 a$ for $z \leq - a$). Using the symmetry of the problem we conclude that
    $$
    \Psi (z) = 2 \pi G \rho_0  \left\{\begin{array}{ll}
    z^2, & | z | < a,\\
    a (2 | z | - a), & | z | \geq a.
    \end{array}\right.
    $$
    The momentum equation reads
    $$
    \rho \frac{\dd \vb{v}}{\dd t} = - \nabla p - \rho \nabla \Psi .
    $$
    For $| z | < a$ this implies that
    $$
    p = - \rho_0 \Psi + \mathrm{const} .
    $$
    The integration constant can be found from the requirement that $p (a) = 0$:
    $$
    0 = p (a) = - 2 \pi G \rho_0^2 a^2 + \mathrm{const} \Longrightarrow
    \mathrm{const} = 2 \pi G \rho_0^2 a^2 .
    $$
    So the pressure is
    $$
    p (z) = 2 \pi G \rho_0^2  \left\{\begin{array}{ll}
    a^2 - z^2, & | z | < a,\\
    0, & | z | \geq a.
    \end{array}\right.
    $$

2.  The equation of motion for a star in the region $| z | \leq a$ is:
    $$
    \ddot{z} (t) = - \partial_z \Psi = - 4 \pi G \rho_0 z = : - \omega^2 z.
    $$
    The general solution is
    $$
    z (t) = A \sin (\omega t) + B \cos (\omega t) .
    $$
    Let's assume that at $t = 0$ the star is passing through the galaxy mid-plane ($z (0) = 0$), then the solution is
    $$
    z (t) = A \sin (\omega t) .
    $$
    We are told that the maximum distance traveled vertically by the star is $a$, so $A = a$. The velocity of the star at the moment it is passing through $z = 0$ is then
    $$
    \dot{z} (0) = [a \omega \cos (\omega t)]_{t = 0} = a \omega \approx 30\,
    \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}} .
    $$
    The period of the oscillation is
    $$
    \frac{2 \pi}{\omega} = \frac{2 \pi}{\sqrt{4 \pi G \rho_0}} \approx 70\,\mathrm{Myr} .
    $$
    This is comparable to the period of the vertical oscillation of the Sun around the mid-plane of the Galaxy, which is estimated to be 60–90 Myr.
:::
:::

::: {#exr-hydro-cloud}
## Mass of a molecular cloud

A self-gravitating cloud of molecular hydrogen $\left( p = nk_B T = \frac{2}{5} \rho \varepsilon \right)$ is measured to have radius $R = 0.1\,\mathrm{pc}$ and temperature $T = 10\,\mathrm{K}$. *Estimate* the mass of the cloud.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
::: {.solution}
We can use the virial theorem:
$$
W + 3 (\Gamma - 1) U = 0.
$$
Assuming the cloud to be spherical and constant density, we have
$$
W = - \frac{3}{5}  \frac{GM^2}{R} .
$$
From the equation of state we have
$$
nk_B T = \frac{2}{5} n \mu m_u \varepsilon \Longrightarrow \varepsilon =
\frac{5}{2}  \frac{k_B T}{\mu m_u} .
$$
The energy content of the cloud is given by
$$
U = \int u \dd V = \int \rho \varepsilon \dd V = \frac{5}{2}  \frac{k_B T}{\mu m_u}
\int \rho \dd V = \frac{5}{2}  \frac{k_B T}{\mu m_u} M.
$$
So we have ($\Gamma = 7 / 5$, $\mu = 2$)
$$
- \frac{3}{5}  \frac{GM^2}{R} + 3 k_B T \frac{M}{\mu m_u} = 0 \Longrightarrow M
= \frac{5 k_B T R}{G \mu m_u} \approx 4.8\,M_{\odot} .
$$
:::
:::

::: {#exr-hydro-sun}
## Temperature of the solar core

Estimate the temperature at the center of the Sun, assuming that density and pressure change over a length scale comparable to the solar radius. Make the estimate twice: first assuming that the Sun is supported by gas pressure, then assuming that it is supported by radiation pressure. Which assumption is more plausible, and why?

Adapted from @clarke2007, Problem 11.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
::: {.solution}
We assume that the density profile of the Sun is given by
$$
\rho (r) = \rho_0  \left( 1 - \frac{r}{R_{\odot}} \right) .
$$
We fix $\rho_0$ by asking that
$$
M_{\odot} = 4 \pi \int_0^{R_{\odot}} \rho (r) r^2 \dd r = \frac{\pi}{3}
R_{\odot}^3 \rho_0 \Longrightarrow \rho_0 = \frac{3 M_{\odot}}{\pi
R_{\odot}^3} \approx \frac{M_{\odot}}{R_{\odot}^3} \approx 6 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}} .
$$
Similarly, we assume that the pressure is given by
$$
p (r) = p_0  \left( 1 - \frac{r}{R_{\odot}} \right) .
$$
The hydrostatic equilibrium condition is
$$
\partial_r p = - \frac{p_0}{R_{\odot}} = - \frac{GM}{r^2} \rho \approx
- \frac{GM_{\odot}}{R_{\odot}^2} \rho_0 \Longrightarrow p_0 = \frac{GM_{\odot}
\rho_0}{R_{\odot}} .
$$
If the Sun is supported by gas pressure, we can estimate its core temperature with the ideal-gas law. Approximating the mean molecular weight to be $\mu = \frac{1}{2}$, we find
$$
\frac{\rho_0}{\frac{1}{2} m_u} k_B T = p_0 = \frac{GM_{\odot}
\rho_0}{R_{\odot}} \Longrightarrow T = \frac{1}{2}  \frac{m_u
GM_{\odot} }{k_B R_{\odot}} \approx 10^7\,\mathrm{K}.
$$
If the pressure is provided by radiation pressure, then we would have
$$
T = \left( \frac{3 GM_{\odot} \rho_0}{aR_{\odot}} \right)^{1 / 4} = \left(
\frac{3 GM_{\odot}^2}{aR_{\odot}^4} \right)^{1 / 4} \approx 4.6 \times 10^7\,
\mathrm{K}.
$$
To decide which assumption is more plausible, we check whether each estimate is consistent. At $T \approx 10^7\,\mathrm{K}$, the radiation pressure is $a T^4 / 3 \approx 3 \times 10^{12}\,\mathrm{Pa}$, less than 1% of $p_0 \approx 1 \times 10^{15}\,\mathrm{Pa}$, so the assumption that the Sun is supported by gas pressure is consistent. At $T \approx 5 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{K}$, instead, the gas pressure would be $\approx 5 \times 10^{15}\,\mathrm{Pa}$, larger than $p_0$, which is a contradiction. We conclude that the Sun is supported by gas pressure.
:::
:::

::: {#exr-hydro-lane-emden}
## Numerical solution of the Lane–Emden equation

The Lane–Emden equation describes the structure of a star with a polytropic equation of state, $p = K \rho^{1 + 1 / n}$. It reads
$$
\frac{1}{\xi^2} \frac{\dd}{\dd \xi} \left( \xi^2 \frac{\dd \theta}{\dd \xi} \right) = - \theta^n, \qquad \theta (0) = 1, \qquad \theta' (0) = 0,
$$ {#eq-hydro-lane-emden}
where $\theta^n$ is the density in units of the central density, and $\xi$ is the radius in suitable units. Write a code to compute numerically the solution of the Lane–Emden equation for a given $n$.

1.  Validate your code by comparing numerical and analytic solution for $n = 0, 1, 5$.

2.  Plot the solution for $n = 1.5$ and find the radius of the polytrope, i.e., the value $\xi_r$ at which $\theta (\xi_r) = 0$.

*Hint:* use the `solve_ivp` function from `scipy.integrate`.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
::: {.solution}
To use `solve_ivp`, we need to convert the Lane–Emden equation into a system of first order equations. This is accomplished by introducing a new variable $\varphi$ such that
$$
\frac{\dd \theta}{\dd \xi} = \varphi, \qquad \frac{\dd
\varphi}{\dd \xi} = - \frac{2 \varphi}{\xi} - \theta^n .
$$
The boundary conditions are $\theta (0) = 1$ and $\varphi (0) = 0$. The latter condition comes from the requirement that $\theta$ should be an even function of $\xi$ (for symmetry). Note that the term $2 \varphi / \xi$ is singular at $\xi = 0$. Close to the center $\theta \approx 1 - \xi^2 / 6$ and $\varphi \approx - \xi / 3$, so $2 \varphi / \xi \rightarrow - 2 / 3$ and $\dd \varphi / \dd \xi \rightarrow - 1 / 3$ as $\xi \rightarrow 0$. For $n = 1.5$ we find $\xi_r \approx 3.654$.

See [`lane-emden.py`](https://github.com/dradice/astrofluids/blob/main/solutions/code/hydrostatic-equilibrium/lane-emden.py) for the implementation.
:::
:::
